items.stem: Define the term "challenge".
items.answer: In Digital Society, a significant problem in the HL extension areas – global well-being, governance and human rights, or sustainable development – that digital systems create or could help address
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: in Digital Society, a significant problem in the HL extension areas – global well-being, governance and human rights, or sustainable development – that digital systems create or could help address. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the context of a challenge must be considered when evaluating an intervention.
items.answer: An intervention that works in one country or community may fail elsewhere because of differences in law, infrastructure, culture, resources and political power.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An intervention that works in one country or community may fail elsewhere because of differences in law, infrastructure, culture, resources and political power. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Paper 3 only tests knowledge of the pre-released statement itself." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The statement sets the topic, but students must apply wider knowledge of real interventions, concepts and stakeholders to unseen material.
items.markingKey: The statement sets the topic, but students must apply wider knowledge of real interventions, concepts and stakeholders to unseen material. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"An intervention that works in one country may not work in another."
— Paraphrase of a common principle in development studies

Explain why this principle is important when evaluating interventions.
items.answer: Context – laws, infrastructure, culture, resources, political systems – affects effectiveness, so evidence from one place may not transfer.
items.markingKey: Context – laws, infrastructure, culture, resources, political systems – affects effectiveness, so evidence from one place may not transfer. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to unpacking a statement on misinformation in elections, explain how it illustrates stakeholder analysis.
items.answer: Students could identify stakeholders (voters, platforms, election bodies, fact-checkers) and interventions (the EU DSA, prebunking campaigns, labels on AI content). Different stakeholders have different powers and interests, which shapes which interventions are feasible.
items.markingKey: Context (Students could identify stakeholders (voters, platforms, election bodies, fact-checkers) and interventions (the EU DSA, prebunking campaigns, labels on AI content).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: different stakeholders have different powers and interests, which shapes which interventions are feasible. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to stakeholder analysis.

items.stem: "Paper 3 only tests knowledge of the pre-released statement itself." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The statement sets the topic, but students must apply wider knowledge of real interventions, concepts and stakeholders to unseen material.
items.markingKey: The statement sets the topic, but students must apply wider knowledge of real interventions, concepts and stakeholders to unseen material. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Global interventions are more effective than local ones in addressing digital challenges."
items.answer: The most effective responses combine global standards with locally adapted implementation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: global problems such as e-waste and platform power cross borders; common standards. Arguments against: local interventions fit context and community needs; global agreements may be weak or slow. Supported judgement: The most effective responses combine global standards with locally adapted implementation.

items.stem: Using a challenge from the HL extension, analyse the interests and power of three stakeholders and how they shape possible interventions.
items.answer: Identify challenge and context; three stakeholders with power/interest; how each enables or blocks interventions; real examples; concepts (power, values); conclusion.
items.markingKey: Identify challenge and context; three stakeholders with power/interest; how each enables or blocks interventions; real examples; concepts (power, values); conclusion.

items.stem: Which Digital Society examination component is taken only by HL students and is based on a pre-released statement?
options: Paper 1
Paper 3
Paper 2
The internal assessment
items.answer: Paper 3
items.markingKey: B. Paper 3 focuses on challenges and interventions.

items.stem: Explain why identifying stakeholders is a key step in unpacking the pre-released statement.
items.answer: The impacts of a challenge and intervention differ between stakeholders, so analysis and recommendations must consider who benefits, who is harmed and who has power to act.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The impacts of a challenge and intervention differ between stakeholders, so analysis and recommendations must consider who benefits, who is harmed and who has power to act. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a primary stakeholder and a secondary stakeholder.
items.answer: Primary stakeholders are directly affected by the challenge or intervention (e.g. users); secondary stakeholders are indirectly affected or influence it (e.g. advertisers, NGOs).
items.markingKey: Primary stakeholders are directly affected by the challenge or intervention (e.g. users); secondary stakeholders are indirectly affected or influence it (e.g. advertisers, NGOs). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A pre-released statement concerns a national ban on smartphones in schools. Stakeholders are scored 1–10 for power and interest: the education ministry (power 3, interest 7); parents (power 1, interest 3); teachers (power 2, interest 9); students (power 8, interest 7). Using a power–interest grid (high = above 5): high power/high interest – manage closely; high power/low interest – keep satisfied; low power/high interest – keep informed; low power/low interest – monitor. Classify each stakeholder.
items.answer: the education ministry – keep informed; parents – monitor; teachers – keep informed; students – manage closely
items.markingKey: the education ministry – keep informed; parents – monitor; teachers – keep informed; students – manage closely [A1 for each pair of correct classifications, max A2]; correct use of the threshold [M1].

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Governments, technology companies and civil society share responsibility for addressing the harms that digital systems can cause."
— Example pre-released statement style, Digital Society HL practice material

Identify three stakeholders mentioned or implied in the statement and explain one responsibility of one of them.
items.answer: Governments, technology companies, civil society; e.g. governments should create and enforce regulation that protects users' rights.
items.markingKey: Governments, technology companies, civil society; e.g. governments should create and enforce regulation that protects users' rights. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "Global interventions are more effective than local ones in addressing digital challenges." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: The most effective responses combine global standards with locally adapted implementation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: global problems such as e-waste and platform power cross borders; common standards. Arguments against: local interventions fit context and community needs; global agreements may be weak or slow. Supported judgement: The most effective responses combine global standards with locally adapted implementation. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Propose a course of action and justify it with reasons and evidence"?
options: recommend
effectiveness
challenge
best-fit approach
items.answer: recommend
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of recommend.

items.stem: Briefly explain why outputs are not the same as outcomes when evaluating interventions.
items.answer: Outputs (devices distributed, posts removed) measure activity; outcomes (learning, reduced harm) measure impact – an intervention can have many outputs and little impact, as with OLPC.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Outputs (devices distributed, posts removed) measure activity; outcomes (learning, reduced harm) measure impact – an intervention can have many outputs and little impact, as with OLPC. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between feasibility and effectiveness.
items.answer: Effectiveness is how well an intervention achieves its aims; feasibility is whether it can practically be implemented given costs, technology, law and support.
items.markingKey: Effectiveness is how well an intervention achieves its aims; feasibility is whether it can practically be implemented given costs, technology, law and support. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Short prebunking videos improved people's ability to recognise manipulation techniques."
— Paraphrase of findings by Roozenbeek et al., Science Advances, 2022

Explain how this evidence could inform a recommendation.
items.answer: A recommendation could scale up prebunking through platforms and schools, while testing how long the effects last.
items.markingKey: A recommendation could scale up prebunking through platforms and schools, while testing how long the effects last. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A student claims: "A good recommendation simply repeats the existing intervention." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It should propose a new or modified step that responds to identified limitations, with justification.
items.markingKey: It should propose a new or modified step that responds to identified limitations, with justification. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A government is choosing an intervention for reducing harm to teenagers on social media. Each option is scored 1–5 (5 = best) on feasibility (weight 0.6), speed of implementation (weight 0.2) and effectiveness (weight 0.2).
age-verification law: feasibility 2, speed of implementation 1, effectiveness 4
default "teen accounts" with limits: feasibility 5, speed of implementation 2, effectiveness 2
school digital-wellbeing lessons: feasibility 5, speed of implementation 5, effectiveness 5
Calculate the weighted score of each option and identify which should be recommended. Explain one limitation of using a weighted matrix to choose an intervention.
items.answer: age-verification law 2.2; default "teen accounts" with limits 3.8; school digital-wellbeing lessons 5; recommend school digital-wellbeing lessons; scores and weights are subjective and may reflect the priorities of decision-makers rather than affected stakeholders; it may hide unintended consequences
items.markingKey: age-verification law: 0.6×2 + 0.2×1 + 0.2×4 = 2.2; default "teen accounts" with limits: 0.6×5 + 0.2×2 + 0.2×2 = 3.8; school digital-wellbeing lessons: 0.6×5 + 0.2×5 + 0.2×5 = 5 [M1 A1 A1]; highest = school digital-wellbeing lessons [A1]. Subjectivity of weights/scores; stakeholder voice; unmeasured effects [R1 R1].

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Bans are an effective intervention for digital challenges."
items.answer: Bans can be effective for narrow, well-defined harms but are usually less effective than design changes and education.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clear and simple; signal social norms (school phone bans). Arguments against: circumvention; removes benefits; enforcement and privacy problems. Supported judgement: Bans can be effective for narrow, well-defined harms but are usually less effective than design changes and education.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that bans are an effective intervention for digital challenges.
items.answer: Bans can be effective for narrow, well-defined harms but are usually less effective than design changes and education.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clear and simple; signal social norms (school phone bans). Arguments against: circumvention; removes benefits; enforcement and privacy problems. Supported judgement: Bans can be effective for narrow, well-defined harms but are usually less effective than design changes and education. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Which is the best evidence that a digital intervention was effective?
options: The cost of the intervention
Measured outcomes compared with a comparison group or baseline
A press release from the company
The number of downloads only
items.answer: Measured outcomes compared with a comparison group or baseline
items.markingKey: B. Outcomes, not outputs, show effectiveness.

items.stem: Distinguish between a strength of an intervention and a limitation.
items.answer: A strength is a feature that helps it achieve its aims (e.g. legally binding); a limitation reduces its effectiveness or causes harm (e.g. easy to circumvent).
items.markingKey: A strength is a feature that helps it achieve its aims (e.g. legally binding); a limitation reduces its effectiveness or causes harm (e.g. easy to circumvent). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "If an intervention has limitations, it should be rejected." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most interventions have limitations; evaluation weighs them against strengths and alternatives and may recommend modifications.
items.markingKey: Most interventions have limitations; evaluation weighs them against strengths and alternatives and may recommend modifications. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to evaluating prebunking campaigns, explain how it illustrates evaluating an educational intervention.
items.answer: Google Jigsaw and university researchers ran short videos teaching manipulation techniques; studies found improved recognition of misinformation techniques, though effects can fade. Evidence-based, low-cost interventions may need repetition to sustain effects.
items.markingKey: Context (Google Jigsaw and university researchers ran short videos teaching manipulation techniques; studies found improved recognition of misinformation techniques, though effects can fade.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: evidence-based, low-cost interventions may need repetition to sustain effects. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evaluating an educational intervention.

items.stem: Evaluate one intervention that addresses a challenge in the HL extension and recommend one further step.
items.answer: Describe intervention and aims; stakeholders; strengths and limitations with evidence; unintended consequences; justified recommendation addressing a limitation.
items.markingKey: Describe intervention and aims; stakeholders; strengths and limitations with evidence; unintended consequences; justified recommendation addressing a limitation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Answering exam-style questions under exam time limits to build pacing and exam technique"?
options: recommend
pre-released statement
timed practice
power–interest grid
items.answer: timed practice
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of timed practice.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Writing more always earns more marks." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Markbands reward quality – focus, evidence, balance and judgement – not length.
items.markingKey: Markbands reward quality – focus, evidence, balance and judgement – not length. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student self-assesses a 12-mark Paper 3 response. It: identifies an intervention and describes it. Using bands 1–3 (limited, general), 4–6 (some analysis, mostly descriptive), 7–9 (evaluation with evidence and some balance) and 10–12 (sustained, balanced evaluation with a well-supported recommendation), identify the most appropriate band and one improvement.
items.answer: Band 1–3; improvement: explain impacts on specific stakeholders
items.markingKey: Band 1–3 [A1] – justified by the features present [R1]; improvement: explain impacts on specific stakeholders [R1].

items.stem: In a practice paper, a student has 90 minutes for 30 marks and plans 5 minutes for reading and planning. Calculate the time per mark for writing and the time to spend on a 8-mark question.
items.answer: 2.83 minutes per mark; about 22.7 minutes

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Self-assessment is as useful as teacher feedback for Paper 3 preparation."
items.answer: Self-assessment is most useful when calibrated with teacher feedback.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: builds independence and understanding of criteria; immediate. Arguments against: students may misjudge their work; teachers have experience of standards. Supported judgement: Self-assessment is most useful when calibrated with teacher feedback.

items.stem: Explain why planning before writing an extended response is valuable.
items.answer: A short plan organises arguments, evidence and stakeholders, ensuring balance and a clear conclusion within the time available.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A short plan organises arguments, evidence and stakeholders, ensuring balance and a clear conclusion within the time available. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Self-assessment always gives an accurate mark.
Reason (R): Students understand markbands better by applying them.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A is false – students can misjudge their work; R is true.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Examiners should use a best-fit approach when deciding the appropriate markband."
— Paraphrase of standard IB markscheme guidance

Explain what a best-fit approach means for students.
items.answer: A response does not need to meet every descriptor perfectly; overall quality decides the band, so strengths in evaluation can compensate for minor gaps.
items.markingKey: A response does not need to meet every descriptor perfectly; overall quality decides the band, so strengths in evaluation can compensate for minor gaps. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

intervention

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "recommend"?

items.stem: Explain why unintended consequences should be considered when evaluating an intervention.
items.answer: Interventions can create new harms – age verification can collect sensitive data, bans can push users to less safe platforms – so judging effectiveness only by intended aims is incomplete.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Interventions can create new harms – age verification can collect sensitive data, bans can push users to less safe platforms – so judging effectiveness only by intended aims is incomplete. items.answer: A point-based markscheme awards marks for specific points; a markband describes overall quality levels and is applied using best fit.
items.markingKey: A point-based markscheme awards marks for specific points; a markband describes overall quality levels and is applied using best fit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: A challenge is the problem (e.g. online harms to children); an intervention is a response to it (e.g. the UK Online Safety Act).
items.markingKey: A challenge is the problem (e.g. online harms to children); an intervention is a response to it (e.g. the UK Online Safety Act). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a recommendation must be justified with reference to the evaluation.
items.answer: A recommendation is convincing only if it addresses the limitations identified and builds on strengths, using evidence about stakeholders and context.

items.stem:
A government is choosing an intervention for protecting journalists from spyware. Each option is scored 1–5 (5 = best) on equity (weight 0.4), feasibility (weight 0.4) and impact on rights (weight 0.2).
export controls on spyware: equity 2, feasibility 1, impact on rights 5
free security audits for journalists: equity 4, feasibility 3, impact on rights 3
a ban on government use of spyware: equity 3, feasibility 2, impact on rights 5
Calculate the weighted score of each option and identify which should be recommended.
items.answer: export controls on spyware 2.2; free security audits for journalists 3.4; a ban on government use of spyware 3; recommend free security audits for journalists
items.markingKey: export controls on spyware: 0.4×2 + 0.4×1 + 0.2×5 = 2.2; free security audits for journalists: 0.4×4 + 0.4×3 + 0.2×3 = 3.4; a ban on government use of spyware: 0.4×3 + 0.4×2 + 0.2×5 = 3 [M1 A1 A1]; highest = free security audits for journalists [A1].

items.stem: With reference to timed Paper 3 practice, explain how it illustrates exam technique.
items.answer: A student practising a past-style Paper 3 allocates time per mark, plans each answer, then self-assesses with markbands and records improvements for the next attempt. Regular timed practice with feedback builds pacing and quality.
items.markingKey: Context (A student practising a past-style Paper 3 allocates time per mark, plans each answer, then self-assesses with markbands and records improvements for the next attempt.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Before a court ruling requiring published reasons for shutdowns was introduced, hours of internet shutdown per year averaged 55. One year later it averaged 24. Calculate the percentage change, and explain why this figure alone cannot prove the intervention was effective.
items.answer: 56.4% decrease; other factors may have changed at the same time (no control group), measurement or reporting may have changed, and a change in the indicator may reflect more reporting rather than more harm
items.markingKey: (24 − 55) ÷ 55 × 100 = -56.4% [M1 A1]; no control/comparison group or confounding factors [R1]; reporting/measurement effects or indicator validity [R1].

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that stakeholder analysis is the most important step in preparing for Paper 3.
items.answer: Stakeholder analysis is essential but must be combined with researched examples and contextual understanding.

Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Regulation is more effective than education as an intervention for online harms." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A combination is most effective: regulation for systemic risks, education for individual resilience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: binding obligations and fines change platform behaviour (DSA); applies at scale. Arguments against: education builds long-term resilience (prebunking); regulation can be circumvented and slow; risks to rights. Supported judgement: A combination is most effective: regulation for systemic risks, education for individual resilience. Markbands (12 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Both true; R explains A.

items.stem: A student claims: "All stakeholders are affected by an intervention in the same way." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Impacts vary – a law can protect users while increasing costs for businesses and restricting some freedoms.
items.markingKey: Impacts vary – a law can protect users while increasing costs for businesses and restricting some freedoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A good recommendation simply repeats the existing intervention." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It should propose a new or modified step that responds to identified limitations, with justification.
items.markingKey: It should propose a new or modified step that responds to identified limitations, with justification. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why self-assessment against markbands improves performance.
items.answer: It shows students what the top band requires (balance, evidence, justified conclusions), helping them identify gaps and target improvements.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows students what the top band requires (balance, evidence, justified conclusions), helping them identify gaps and target improvements. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe unpacking a statement on online harms to children and explain what it reveals about unpacking a challenge.
items.answer: A pre-released statement on children's online safety could be unpacked by identifying the challenge (exposure to harmful content), stakeholders (children, parents, platforms, regulators) and interventions (UK Online Safety Act, Australia's under-16 social-media ban, Instagram Teen Accounts). Mapping challenge, stakeholders and interventions creates a framework for evaluation.

items.stem: With reference to evaluating the EU Digital Services Act, explain how it illustrates evaluating regulation.
items.answer: The DSA (fully applicable from 2024) requires transparency, risk assessments and audits for very large platforms, with fines up to 6% of global turnover. Its strengths are binding obligations; limitations include enforcement capacity and global reach.

items.stem: With reference to peer marking with markbands, explain how it illustrates assessment literacy.
items.answer: Students swap 12-mark responses, apply best fit using the markband, and justify the band with evidence from the response. Applying markbands deepens understanding of what examiners reward.

items.stem: A pre-released statement concerns a right-to-repair law for electronics. Stakeholders are scored 1–10 for power and interest: environmental groups (power 2, interest 8); legislators (power 2, interest 9); independent repair shops (power 4, interest 4); consumers (power 4, interest 8). Using a power–interest grid (high = above 5): high power/high interest – manage closely; high power/low interest – keep satisfied; low power/high interest – keep informed; low power/low interest – monitor. Classify each stakeholder.
items.answer: environmental groups – keep informed; legislators – keep informed; independent repair shops – monitor; consumers – keep informed
items.markingKey: environmental groups – keep informed; legislators – keep informed; independent repair shops – monitor; consumers – keep informed [A1 for each pair of correct classifications, max A2]; correct use of the threshold [M1].

items.stem:
A government is choosing an intervention for closing the rural connectivity gap. Each option is scored 1–5 (5 = best) on impact on rights (weight 0.5), feasibility (weight 0.3) and speed of implementation (weight 0.2).
satellite broadband vouchers: impact on rights 1, feasibility 2, speed of implementation 5
community Wi-Fi hubs: impact on rights 4, feasibility 3, speed of implementation 3
subsidised mobile data plans: impact on rights 2, feasibility 2, speed of implementation 5
Calculate the weighted score of each option and identify which should be recommended.
items.answer: satellite broadband vouchers 2.1; community Wi-Fi hubs 3.5; subsidised mobile data plans 2.6; recommend community Wi-Fi hubs
items.markingKey: satellite broadband vouchers: 0.5×1 + 0.3×2 + 0.2×5 = 2.1; community Wi-Fi hubs: 0.5×4 + 0.3×3 + 0.2×3 = 3.5; subsidised mobile data plans: 0.5×2 + 0.3×2 + 0.2×5 = 2.6 [M1 A1 A1]; highest = community Wi-Fi hubs [A1].

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Regulation is more effective than education as an intervention for online harms."
items.answer: A combination is most effective: regulation for systemic risks, education for individual resilience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: binding obligations and fines change platform behaviour (DSA); applies at scale. Arguments against: education builds long-term resilience (prebunking); regulation can be circumvented and slow; risks to rights. Supported judgement: A combination is most effective: regulation for systemic risks, education for individual resilience.

items.stem: "Self-assessment is as useful as teacher feedback for Paper 3 preparation." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Self-assessment is most useful when calibrated with teacher feedback.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: builds independence and understanding of criteria; immediate. Arguments against: students may misjudge their work; teachers have experience of standards. Supported judgement: Self-assessment is most useful when calibrated with teacher feedback. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Global interventions are more effective than local ones in addressing digital challenges." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The most effective responses combine global standards with locally adapted implementation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: global problems such as e-waste and platform power cross borders; common standards. Arguments against: local interventions fit context and community needs; global agreements may be weak or slow. Supported judgement: The most effective responses combine global standards with locally adapted implementation. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: "Bans are an effective intervention for digital challenges." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Bans can be effective for narrow, well-defined harms but are usually less effective than design changes and education.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: clear and simple; signal social norms (school phone bans). Arguments against: circumvention; removes benefits; enforcement and privacy problems. Supported judgement: Bans can be effective for narrow, well-defined harms but are usually less effective than design changes and education. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.
